#3397. 32 Years Later, Star Trek's Most Important Movie Is Officially Free on Streaming

There are few things Star Trek fans love more than a good crossover. Bringing together characters from different eras of the franchise is practically guaranteed to generate excitement, particularly when those characters happen to be two of Starfleet's most legendary captains. But what happens when the movie designed to unite them doesn't quite live up to expectations?

Released in 1994 and now streaming free on Pluto TV, Star Trek: Generations brought Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) and Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) together on the big screen for the first and only time. The result was a movie that divided fans, delivered one of the franchise's most controversial deaths, and destroyed one of television's most beloved starships. Yet more than three decades later, Generations deserves another look, particularly for what it has to say about growing older, accepting loss, and knowing when it's time to move on.

The film opens with Kirk, Montgomery Scott (James Doohan), and Pavel Chekov (Walter Koenig) attending the maiden voyage of the Enterprise-B. Kirk is retired, although it's obvious he hasn't entirely adjusted to life outside the captain's chair.

When Kirk discovers that the ship's helmsman is Demora Sulu (Jacqueline Kim), daughter of his former crewmate Hikaru Sulu (George Takei), he's surprised his old friend found time to start a family. Scotty reminds him of something Kirk himself has always said: If something is important, you make the time.

It's a seemingly insignificant exchange that establishes one of the movie's central themes. Kirk has spent his life exploring the galaxy, but what has he missed along the way? He's saved countless lives and made history, yet he's struggling to find purpose without the Enterprise.

Decades later, Picard faces his own reckoning with mortality after learning that his brother Robert and nephew René have died in a fire. The tragedy leaves him confronting the possibility that his family line will end with him, along with the realization that the life he chose came at the expense of another he might have had.

Both captains eventually find themselves inside the Nexus, a mysterious energy ribbon that offers its inhabitants a seemingly perfect existence. For Picard, that means experiencing the family life he never had. Kirk finds himself back in a peaceful home, with the opportunity to reconnect with a woman from his past. Perhaps Edith Keeler?

The temptation is understandable. Who wouldn't want the chance to revisit a happier moment or correct a regret? But Generations makes the case that a meaningful life isn't necessarily a perfect one. Sometimes it's the choices we make, and the sacrifices that come with them, that give our lives purpose.

None of this means Generations is without problems. Far from it. The movie's villain, Dr. Tolian Soran (Malcolm McDowell), wants to return to the Nexus so badly he's willing to destroy entire star systems to make it happen. While McDowell brings considerable menace to the role, Soran never quite becomes the memorable antagonist the story needs.

Then there's Kirk's death, which remains one of the most debated moments in Star Trek history. After surviving Klingons, Romulans, Khan, and countless other threats, the legendary captain meets his end beneath a collapsing bridge. For a character who spent decades boldly going where no one had gone before, it's not exactly the grand farewell many fans imagined. And yet there's plenty here to appreciate.

Stewart delivers some of his finest work as Picard struggles with grief, particularly during a quiet conversation with Counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis). The destruction of the Enterprise-D is also genuinely shocking, especially for viewers who spent seven seasons watching the ship become almost as much a character as the people aboard it.

There's also the introduction of Data's (Brent Spiner) emotion chip, which provides some welcome humor, even if the movie occasionally leans a little too heavily into the android's newfound feelings.

Most importantly, Shatner and Stewart make the film's long-awaited meeting worthwhile. Their scenes together aren't built around elaborate action sequences or clever one-liners. Instead, they feature two captains reflecting on what it means to make a difference. It's a quieter approach than some viewers might have expected, but one that feels appropriate for these characters.

Beyond its story, Generations occupies a unique place in Star Trek history. It was the franchise's first theatrical film built around the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation, arriving just months after the television series concluded its seven-season run.

For years, Kirk and his crew had been the faces of Star Trek on the big screen. Now it was Picard's turn. The movie makes that transition literal. Kirk begins the film as a celebrated former captain watching a new Enterprise depart without him. By the conclusion, he's helping Picard save millions of lives and making one final sacrifice before leaving the future in another captain's hands.

The destruction of the Enterprise-D reinforces that transition. The ship that carried Picard and his crew through seven seasons of television adventures is gone, clearing the way for a new chapter. The Next Generation cast would return in three more films, beginning with 1996's Star Trek: First Contact.

There's something fitting about a movie so concerned with the passage of time serving as the bridge between two eras of Star Trek. The franchise was changing, just as its characters were learning to accept change in their own lives.

Generations may not be the best Star Trek movie, but beneath the spectacle, questionable decisions, and collapsing bridges is a thoughtful story about two men who devoted their lives to making a difference. When Kirk gets one last opportunity to do exactly that, he doesn't hesitate. For all the movie's imperfections, it's hard to imagine a more appropriate final choice for the captain of the Enterprise.

Star Trek Generations is free to streaming Pluto TV. You can also watch it on Paramount Plus.

#3396. Keychron just ended the magnetic vs. mechanical keyboard debate: the V6 Ultra Hybrid proves you can have both with literally no compromises and even a magnetic tactile switch

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Someone had to do dual MX/HE compatibility properly, and Keychron stepped up to the mark. The Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE offers dual magnetic and mechanical switch compatibility, plus the widest array of magnetic hot-swappability I’ve yet seen. It’s formidable for gaming, beautiful for typing, built well and reasonably priced. It’s a little bland-looking, but that’s a minor point, and we had a small QC issue, although I’d expect that to be fixed in full production units.

Minor QC issues (hopefully fixed by full production)

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE (catchy name, right?) attempts to forge ‘The One Ring’ of keyboards. One keyboard to rule them all, to do and be everything for everyone. The master keyboard.

As such, it’s the latest in a very small selection of keyboards that offer dual mechanical and magnetic capability. If you want to hot-swap from magnetic back to mechanical switches, you can. But the V6 takes things further with, as I alluded to above, an altogether more holistic approach. The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE also packs everything else Keychron has to throw at a keyboard — which essentially means every feature that actually exists right now.

8K polling, tons of magnetic features and customization in the Launcher app, gasket mounting for comfortable typing — all with a reasonable price tag. It also offers my holy grail feature at checkout: a magnetic and tactile switch, for elite gaming and typing without even needing to hot-swap in the first place.

So, like, is this legitimately the perfect hybrid board? The best gaming keyboard and the best mechanical keyboard all rolled into one? I think so. Keychron has done it. Find out more in my full Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE review.

Where to even start? Proper MX/HE hot swap, bags of gaming and productivity performance, reasonable price — this is a Goldilocks keyboard.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE’s main feature is denoted by the “Hybrid” part of its (terribly convoluted) name. This board is dual mechanical/magnetic switch compatible, meaning you can swap between the two.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid takes any standard 3-pin or 5-pin mechanical switches. It also supports a wide range of magnetic switches with the N Pole facing downwards — that means Gateron x Wooting Jade switches, Gateron KS-20 switches, and any of Gateron’s ever-growing line of dual rail magnetic switches. Neat.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Now Keychron isn’t the first to do dual MX/HE. Glorious did it a while back with the hilariously overpriced GMMK 3 HE. More recently, Lofree had a pop with the Hyzen, but with typically Lofree results: great looks and typing but rank amateurism in the software department (pivotal to a magnetic board). Keychron, in usual Keychron fashion, is the first to do a proper job of it, with the widest magnetic hot-swap scope while still keeping things affordable.

The long and short is that the V6 Ultra Hybrid has more actual hot-swap potential than any other magnetic board that I know of. Most magnetic boards claim to be hot swappable, but only support a couple of switch variants from the same specific magnetic switch line — often the variants available at checkout. In reality, that usually makes hot-swap claims severely hamstrung at best; meaningless at worst. Not so here. Again, the Lofree Hyzen also supports an impressive roster of compatible magnetic switches, but lacks the professional polish of Keychron’s boards.

The “hybrid” moniker also has another related meaning. The V6 Ultra Hybrid is a hybrid board for both work and play, offering powerful gaming performance while capable enough to handle the rigors of work and heavy typing.

The bit that excites me most are two of the magnetic switch choices available from stock. The V6 Ultra Hybrid ships with one of four Gateron Ultra Fast Lime magnetic switches, two of which are tactile. Yes, tactile magnetic switches — this is the biggest news in my opinion.

All magnetic switches up to now have been linear in operation. Sure, being able to hot-swap those is fine, but swapping out 108 switches from a full-sized keyboard is a ginormous time suck. So it’s not like you can just quickly switch from tactiles for work to magnetic for gaming. If, like me, you enjoy tactile switches but want magnetic gaming performance, you’ve so far been left out in the cold. Not anymore.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid also packs plenty of Keychron’s productivity heritage. There’s a gasket mount, for bouncy and comfortable typing; Keychron’s steeply-raked and deeply-sculpted OSA profile keycaps, which I find ideal for fast typing; and screw-in stabilizers for minimal big key wobble. As you can see, my typing speed and accuracy were both above average on the V6 Ultra Hybrid, helped by paring back the actuation to 2.6mm — my personal sweet spot and where I type-test all magnetic boards. I could (and indeed did) type on this thing all day.

Thanks to Gateron’s magnetic switches, you also get every elite gaming feature under the sun right now: adjustable actuation; rapid trigger; dynamic keystroke for multiple commands per actuation; custom SOCD resolutions for last key prioritization (A.K.A. ‘Snap Tap’). There’s 8K polling too, although on a keyboard this is tantamount to snake oil, if you ask me. All of this is customizable through Keychron’s fantastic web launcher.

I used the board for everything, from competitive gaming on “Counter-Strike 2” and “Wardogs,” through to more relaxed titles like “Total War: Rome II,” “Valheim,” and “Dune: Awakening.” It never put a foot wrong.

Admittedly, if you want a board purely for competitive FPS gaming, you’re probably better off with a plate-, tray-, or top-mounted magnetic board like the NuPhy Air60 HE, NuPhy Field75 HE, or Keychron Q16 HE 8K — these mount styles aren’t as comfortable, but move around less than a gasket mount, making them less likely to cause accidental inputs at super low <0.5mm switch actuations.

If you need an all-rounder for both work and play, though, I seriously can’t think of a better board than the V6 Ultra Hybrid.

As this is a Keychron board, you get all the expected goodies. Aside from some QC issues I’ll cover later, the board is built well, using premium materials. The case is sturdy ABS plastic with very little bend and flex — impressive given this is a long board.

The keycaps are doubleshot PBT, which will stand up well to wear and tear without going shiny, unlike ABS keycaps. PBT is also grease resistant. I did my usual test, typing on the keyboard after eating Monster Munch (a fried corn snack here in the U.K.), and the V6’s keycaps picked up a lot of grease but were easy to wipe down. Not quite as impressive as the caps on the Logitech G Pro X2 Rapid, which completely resisted the same grease altogether — like not even a single smear.

The V6 features a decent 4,000mAh battery, plus triple Bluetooth, 2.4G and wired connectivity, toggleable via a switch on the case. There’s a macOS/Windows toggle, too, but Keychron still supplies separate sets of Windows and macOS command keys rather than dual-labeling its keycaps. This is a longstanding frustration of mine. I switch between the two OS’ constantly for work. It’s great to have the toggle, but it undermines the ease if I have to switch keycaps too. A small issue, but one that’s so easily solvable by dual labelling — as proved by the Lofree Hyzen and Lofree Flow 2.

When I reviewed the original Keychron V6, which I awarded a full five stars, one of my favorite features was the price. It offered major performance for a very reasonable sum. The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is pricier. It costs $164 versus the $99 basic V6 and the $119 V6 Ultra (which has faster polling, better internal damping, nicer switches, etc — just an all-round upgraded package).

However, the V6 Ultra Hybrid packs a lot more functionality than the lower-tier V6 models thanks to the dual MX/HE switch compatibility, and way more gaming features when using HE switches. An extra $45 over the standard V6 Ultra is fair game for all that, at least in my book.

Let’s look at the hybrid MX/HE competition, too. The Lofree Hyzen costs a whopping $279 — sure it’s made from aluminum and is beautiful to behold, but the software is janky as hell. The Glorious GMMK 3 HE starts at $179, but you can easily get up to near $500 for choice productivity upgrades (and to make it look less ugly than stock). By those two yardsticks, the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is the best value-for-money hybrid board on the market, and it ain’t even close.

At the time of writing, the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is in pre-order, after its Kickstarter campaign, with estimated shipping starting December 2026.

As I’ve mentioned in previous reviews, I absolutely hate that Keychron floats its new boards on Kickstarter. Keychron is a major keyboard brand (arguably the dominant productivity market force) that absolutely does not need to crowdfund its boards. Besides, as someone who has tested several of Keychron’s crowdfunded boards, I can tell you they’re already developed and practically finished by the start of the campaigns (because most Keychron boards are 95% the same under the hood). Oh well. That’s just unfortunately how Keychron chooses to operate, but you can rest assured that there’s usually very little chance of a crowdfunding rug pull from this brand.

There’s very little I don’t like about the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE, aside from its ridiculously long-winded name. It’s a little boring to look at, I guess, and I saw some QC teething issues, but nothing that should seriously dissuade you.

Ah, look: black plastic case, gray rounded keycaps, a tiny bit of color on the ESC key. It must be a Keychron! Yawn. I’m not saying the V6 Ultra Hybrid is bad-looking, but it’s the same old Keychron design we’ve seen for years now. And it’s getting kinda boring.

Now, as someone who has owned, tested, used, or edited the reviews of literally hundreds of keyboards, this probably affects me more than you. I see a lot of Keychrons; you’ll probably only see the one you buy.

But man, I wish Keychron would make some more exciting decks in its more affordable V- and K-series sometimes. Pretty boards with plenty of color, like the NuPhy Halo75; or handsome futuristic designs like the Lofree Hyzen and Lofree Block. Come on, Keychron, spice it up a bit.

As Keychron has grown, I’ve seen firsthand its once stellar reputation for build quality start to drop. A few years ago, every single Keychron board we tested was built like a tank. Now we’re seeing frequent issues with sticky switches or other build quality concerns. Not all the time, I must say. And Keychron is always keen to hear from us when this happens, so we always tell its representatives and receive a replacement in quick order. But it’s getting to the point now that I’m seeing a pattern I can’t ignore.

My first V6 Ultra Hybrid review unit suffered both a sticky switch (solved by adjusting debounce time) and a USB dongle port that was far too large with no magnet inside, meaning the 2.4G receiver would fall out. Keychron’s representative has assured me this was a pre-production teething issue, and issued me a full production unit where the problem has been fixed. But as I said above, similar issues are becoming too common now from this once wholly reliable brand, and it’s a problem I need to call out. Keychron, if you’re reading, please step your game back up.

I utterly adore this keyboard. I won’t be using it long-term because I prefer a 75% layout (so I‘m eagerly waiting for a V2 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE). But I absolutely love what this deck signifies.

As is so often the case in the productivity keyboard arena, it takes Keychron to turn its attention to an innovation to truly bring that feature into the mainstream and make it work. Dual MX/HE compatibility is now here, with proper wide-ranging switch support for both mechanical and magnetic. And there’s a tactile magnetic switch on offer to boot.

If you want one keyboard that excels for literally every purpose, without breaking the bank, it’s the Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE. End of story.

#3395. Ridley Scott's Blade Runner Used Extra Footage From A Stanley Kubrick Movie

In the American theatrical version of Ridley Scott's 1982 sci-fi film "Blade Runner," the film had a happy ending for Rick and Rachael.

This was an alteration made to "Blade Runner" after Scott's original cut was not well-received by test audiences. Scott's intended ending involved a weirdly symbolic image of a character examining a piece of origami folded into a unicorn, and Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) walking into an elevator with the replicant Rachael (Sean Young). The ending was ambiguous and downbeat, in the spirit of film noir.

Scott recalled the experience in a 2015 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, saying that an unnamed investor wanted him to tack on a happy ending where Rick and Rachel drive off into the woods together. In the happy ending, Rick talks in voiceover about how Rachel is a special kind of replicant who can live indefinitely. Harrison Ford is on record about how much he hates that voiceover.

There have been many cuts of "Blade Runner" over the years, and Scott has been very frank about how much he dislikes the "happy ending" that was mandated to him.

Despite the frustration, though, Scott followed orders from his investors. To make that happy ending, Scott consulted with fellow director Stanley Kubrick and managed to get some of Kubrick's footage that was shot for the opening credits of his 1980 horror film "The Shining." The "happy ending" of "Blade Runner" featured a high shot of a lovely wilderness as Rick and Rachael drive off into the woods together. That was actually reused "Shining" footage, granted to Scott with Kubrick's blessing.

Stanley Kubrick had previously cold-called Ridley Scott after Kubrick watched "Alien" for the first time, wondering how the heck Scott had pulled off one of that film's most memorable moments. That call began their relationship as colleagues.

Scott remembered the whole experience borrowing "The Shining" footage, explaining:

"I had finished Blade Runner, and it was a disaster. My investors were giving me a really hard time, saying 'You can't end the film with picking up a piece of origami, looking at the girl, walk in the elevator, nod, and bingo that's it.' I said, 'It's called a film noir.' And they said, 'What's a film noir?' That was a big problem. And he said, 'We have to test this with an uplifting ending, where they will go off into the wilderness together.' I said, 'Well if they go off into a beautiful wilderness, why do they live in this dystopian environment?'"

Scott then said he asked Stanley Kubrick for a little of that lovely woodsy footage he shot for "The Shining" and inserted it into "Blade Runner." He continued:

"By then I had talked to Stanley a few times. I said, 'I know you shot the hell out of 'The Shining,' can I have some of the stuff?' So at the end of the film in 'Blade Runner,' that's Stanley Kubrick's footage."

Of course, the cut of "Blade Runner" that used footage from "The Shining" was eventually abandoned in favor of the more popular Director's Cut. To orient you on all the jiggery-pokery that went down with "Blade Runner," /Film has assembled a guide to the film's multiple endings. It's ... a lot.

And then, after all that, Kubrick was said to have hated "Blade Runner" regardless.

Sarah Maitland, who spent a spell collaborating with Kubrick on his never-completed version of "A.I. Artificial Intelligence," spoke with Far Out Magazine in 2025, and recalled a time when Kubrick talked about "Blade Runner," and how the movie was kind of pointless. Half the movie, Kubrick said, was devoted to solving whether or not Rachael was a replicant, and Kubrick felt that if no one could tell the difference, then why bother with anything? "[I]f they can't tell," Maitland recalled Kubrick saying, "why do they think it matters? There is nothing in that film that suggests for one second why it should matter."

Kubrick was a pal for lending Scott that "Shining" footage, but nothing he did made "Blade Runner" a better movie.

#3394. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

#3393. Slow Horses Star Jack Lowden Was In Dwayne Johnson's Most Underrated Movie

We just saw Jack Lowden wrap up another successful season of "Slow Horses," in which his character, River Cartwright, reunited with a former love. It was one of the most surprisingly tender installments of the best spy show on TV, with "Slow Horses" Season 6 immediately improving on Season 5 by embracing a darker overall tone (while still maintaining the series' signature sardonic wit). Those who particularly enjoyed this latest season might be intrigued to know that Lowden previously starred in a film that similarly combined a heartfelt emotional core with a dry wit: "Fighting with My Family."

To be clear, this 2019 biographical sports dramedy is nothing like "Slow Horses" in terms of its genre and tone. But it does mix naturalistic drama, action, humor, and heart in a similar fashion to the spy series. That's not too surprising considering the film was written and directed by Stephen Merchant and "Slow Horses" was overseen for its first five seasons by Will Smith, both of whom came up in the British comedy scene of the early 2000s. Merchant is, of course, best known for co-creating "The Office" with Ricky Gervais, while Smith was a writer for, and starred in, the BBC sitcom "The Thick of It."

Another thing tying these two projects together (aside from both being set in England) is Lowden, who delivers one of his most underrated performances in "Fighting with My Family." It also has The Rock in it, if that sort of thing appeals. In fact, the film is also one of Dwayne Johnson's most underrated movies, even if he isn't actually in it all that much.

"Fighting with My Family" is based on the 2012 documentary "The Wrestlers: Fighting with My Family." The film saw director Max Fisher spend a year following the Knight family of Norfolk, who run the World Association of Wrestling from their suburban home. The doc particularly focused on the Knights' daughter, Saraya-Jade Bevis, as she tried out for the WWE. That story, it seems, caught the attention of Dwayne Johnson, who teamed up with Stephen Merchant to give Bevis' story the big screen treatment.

In 2019, Merchant spoke to /Film about "Fighting with My Family," recalling how he'd acted with Johnson in 2010's "Tooth Fairy" and had "got along well" with the wrestler turned actor. The pair evidently stayed in touch, which ultimately led to their collaboration on "Fighting with My Family," which Johnson executive produced and appeared in. "I have no particular interest in wrestling and didn't know anything about it," admitted Merchant. "[Johnson] happened to see a documentary while in Britain filming 'Fast & Furious 6.'" This was the genesis of "Fighting with My Family." After Johnson became acquainted with Bevis via WWE, he reached out to Merchant to write and direct. The comedian accepted.

The film he wrote similarly follows the career of English wrestler Saraya Knight/Paige, played by Florence Pugh, as she works towards a career in WWE. Jack Lowden plays her brother, Zak Knight/Zak Zodiac, who has similar dreams of making it to the big leagues. Only Saraya earns a spot in the WWE's training program, however, and she is forced to leave her family behind to pursue her dreams.

As /Film's Ethan Anderton wrote in his review, "Fighting with My Family" gives WWE fans the movie they deserve. But this is more than a wrestling movie. It's also a heartfelt comedy drama that boasts great performances from both Florence Pugh and Jack Lowden. "Slow Horses" fans should get a kick out of seeing Lowden as Zak Knight. Whereas River Cartwright is the upper-middle class son of a former MI5 head, Zak is a determined youngster who grew up in a council house. It's interesting to see how the Scottish actor renders the latter in comparison to his other best-known role.

Lena Headey and Nick Frost play Zak and Saraya's parents Ricky and Julia Knight, and both of them have a great time in their roles. Then there is, of course, The Rock, who shows up a couple times throughout the movie and is, well, The Rock. Beyond his cameos, though, Dwayne Johnson was invested in the story and did a great job shepherding the project to fruition — as evidenced by the critical response.

"Fighting with My Family" earned a 93% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes and a $41.5 million take at the global box office on an $11 million budget. All in all, then, it was a success, even if it didn't become a major hit with a massive cultural impact. Now, Lowden is said to be one of five finalists to become the new James Bond, so if you want to acquaint yourself with the actor's filmography ahead of what might be the biggest moment of his career, "Fighting with My Family" is a great place to start. The film is available to watch for free on Tubi.

#3392. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3391. League of Legends: New Dawn Revealed, Major Overhaul Set for 2027

The evolution of the long-running MOBA will get a full reveal in January

Between matches at the 2026 League of Legends World Championship, Riot Games teased fans with a long-anticipated announcement: The next era of League of Legends is upon us.

Revealed in an array of cinematics and gameplay, the “all-encompassing, large-scale update” coming to the 17-year-old game in 2027 is titled New Dawn. If the cheers that bellowed through the Barclays Center in Brooklyn are any indication, diehard fans of the franchise are ready.

Riot left most details of this major overhaul to the imagination. The cinematic trailer for New Dawn revealed stunning renders of several fan-favorite champions, including Blitzcrank, Lux, Leona, Sett, Poppy, Volibear, Riven, Jhin, and Ahri. Snippets of gameplay saw Master Yi and Morgana in action. But what is at the heart of the update? The studio says it will have more to reveal in January.

What the announcement did reveal is that League will get a brand-new game client in 2027; Riot last overhauled the architecture in 2016. The sizzle reel also promised a refreshed version of the Summoner’s Rift map, a defining feature of the long-running MOBA. For now, fans can only speculate what Riot’s description of “evolved gameplay, and new ways to experience players’ favorite champions” really means.

Whatever the case, there’s a clear ambition on Riot’s part to grow the game not only for longtime players but a potentially new audience that may only know League from Arcane or the Riftbound TCG. At a pre-Finals press event, League executive producer Paul Bellezza made it very clear that Riot sees the game as “multi-generational” and would love for it to run “100 years.” Doing that requires strategy. At a time when major live-service franchises are also gunning for expanded and renewed attention (see: World of Warcraft: Forever), it’s only natural that Riot would follow suit with League.

But the company isn’t ready to share their real game plan just yet. Instead, it bundled announcements of a new vision for gameplay with a reminder that League remains a major esports endeavor. Next year’s calendar will see some bigger changes too: The 2027 season kicks off in China with an expanded First Stand tournament, followed by the Mid-Season Invitational in Valencia, Spain. Worlds 2027 will span Japan and South Korea, with Nagoya hosting Japan’s first-ever World Championship matches before the tournament concludes in Seoul. Riot is also considering replacing the traditional Worlds Play-In Stage with the Demacia Cup, potentially opening the door for more teams to compete.

#3390. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3387. Why Doctor Strange Abandons The Avengers To Join Doctor Doom Explained

There's a sensible reason why Doctor Strange betrays the Avengers and becomes Doctor Doom's right-hand man during the collapse of the Marvel multiverse. Every major Avengers antagonist has led an army and a group of devoted lieutenants. In The Avengers, Loki weaponizes the Chitauri to invade the Earth, assisted by the brainwashed Hawkeye and Erik Selvig. In Avengers: Age of Ultron, Ultron builds an endless hive-mind swarm of Ultron Sentries designed to evolve alongside him and enlists Wanda and Pietro Maximoff before the twins defect. When Thanos finally makes his move in Infinity War and Endgame, he brings the Black Order and hordes of Outriders and Chitauri with him.

One of the biggest questions surrounding Avengers: Doomsday is the identity of Doctor Doom's acolytes, who seem to draw inspiration from the Black Swans and Black Priests of Jonathan Hickman’s Time Runs Out storyline. While there's a possibility they're Doombots or alternate Victor von Doom variants, close inspection of their masks and cloaks suggests that Doom is secretly leading corrupted or brainwashed variants of MCU magic users. Doctor Strange, Wanda Maximoff, Clea, and Sylvie are the most likely heroes-turned-villains hiding behind the hoods, potentially manipulated into believing that Doom's authoritarian rule is the only way to save a collapsing multiverse from total destruction.

Marvel Studios inevitably makes significant changes to every major comic book storyline it adapts into live-action, and the plot of Time Runs Out and Secret Wars is no exception. Just like the exact location of the Infinity Stones ahead of Avengers: Infinity War and the Avengers' method to undo Thanos' Snap ahead of Avengers: Endgame, the mystery behind Doctor Doom's followers might be one of Avengers: Doomsday's biggest points of speculation and one of its biggest twists as well.

As the Marvel multiverse collapses in Jonathan Hickman’s Secret Wars saga, Doctor Strange realizes that neither the Illuminati nor the Avengers can prevent the end of all existence. Throughout the preceding Time Runs Out storyline, Strange watches brilliant minds like Reed Richards and Tony Stark exhaust every scientific and ethical option while incursions erase entire realities. Having already abandoned conventional superhero morality by embracing dark blood magic to save his world, Strange ultimately discovers that the omnipotent Beyonders are orchestrating the multiverse's destruction.

Doctor Strange uncovers Victor von Doom’s secret identity as Rabum Alal, the Great Destroyer who spent years killing Molecule Men across parallel worlds before gathering the survivors into a massive bomb to use against the Beyonders. Doom embraced the unthinkable role of cosmic executioner to buy creation a fighting chance. So, joining forces with Doom and Molecule Man for a last stand against the Beyonders before the final universes collide, Strange witnesses Owen Reece channel the Ivory Kings' godlike energy into Victor.

Following Doctor Doom's creation of Battleworld, Doctor Strange cements his choice to support Doom and accepts the role of Sheriff Strange, willingly partnering with Doom so that at least a sliver of humanity survives. Strange knows deep down that Victor is a tyrant whose rule will eventually crumble under his own pride, but he also understands that without Doom’s iron grip, nothing would exist at all. Although Strange's support of God Emperor Doom is a betrayal of his heroic principles, he has no option but to help a ruthless monarch hold the pieces together until a better world can be reborn.

As Sheriff of Battleworld, Doctor Strange becomes the supreme enforcer and right-hand magistrate of the realm, bearing the exhausting burden of keeping Victor von Doom’s patchwork reality from tearing itself apart. Based in Battleworld's Isle of Agamotto, Strange leads the Thor Corps and mediates violent border disputes between rival barons like Sinister, Apocalypse, and Maestro. Whenever rebellions erupt or forbidden memories of the old multiverse resurface, Sheriff Strange arrives to restore stability. Besides, Strange also hides the sealed life raft of surviving Earth-616 heroes he discovered years after Battleworld's creation, keeping the mysterious vessel locked away to prevent it from affecting the peace while he outwardly enforces Doom's every decree.

After eight years of enforcing Battleworld’s laws, Sheriff Strange turns against God Emperor Doom during the explosive climax of Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribić’s Secret Wars #4. Strange had secretly kept the mysterious Earth-616 life raft hidden inside his Isle of Agamotto sanctum for five years after discovering it, unsure of what lay inside. When a separate raft belonging to the sinister Cabal led by Thanos and the Maker breaches Battleworld, Strange finally has the Earth-616 vessel opened, awakening Reed Richards, Spider-Man, Black Panther, Captain Marvel, Star-Lord, Cyclops, and the Mighty Thor to join him in the fray.

The Battleworld conflict draws God Emperor Doom himself down to the battlefield, where the omnipotent ruler kills Cyclops and confronts Sheriff Strange. Then, Strange performs a powerful teleportation spell that scatters Reed Richards, Black Panther, and the rest of the surviving heroes safely across Battleworld’s various domains where they can ignite a coordinated rebellion. Shockingly, after Strange mocks Doom's lingering fear of Richards, God Emperor Doom obliterates Strange on the spot with a single blast, making Strange a martyr whose final spell ensures the downfall of Doom's empire.

The MCU captured the spirit of Doctor Strange’s pragmatic compromise in Avengers: Infinity War, when he voluntarily handed the Time Stone over to Thanos on Titan. Although Strange's decision is now seen as the wise first step in his successful plan to overturn Thanos' Snap and bring half of the universe back to life, it used to seem like an uncharacteristic move from one of the MCU's brightest minds. Just like his Secret Wars counterpart, Benedict Cumberbatch's MCU Strange recognized that outright victory at that moment was impossible and that temporary defeat was the sole pathway to survival.

Since the MCU has already shown Strange willingly hand victory to a tyrant once, Avengers: Doomsday will likely adapt Sheriff Strange with a clever twist so the beat doesn't feel repetitive. Instead of having Earth-616 Strange consciously strike another secret bargain with Doctor Doom, the MCU's adaptation of Time Runs Out and Secret Wars could introduce a brainwashed Strange who may have lost an off-screen battle against Doom following the events of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. This scenario is more likely, considering the rest of Doctor Doom's acolytes are also likely to be fellow Avengers.

How do you think Avengers: Doomsday will adapt Doctor Strange's allegiance to Doctor Doom?

#3386. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3385. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

#3384. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”
