#3383. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3382. John Wick Meets Reacher In This Must-Read Thriller That Keanu Reeves Is Adapting Next

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

After starring in the John Wick film franchise and witnessing the success of the Jack Reacher adaptations, Keanu Reeves' next major movie project will blend the two seamlessly using an exciting new title as its foundation. The best action thrillers in recent memory have managed to combine a strong story from the central character, creating compelling stakes that feel bigger than simple survival. With most of the protagonists in the action thriller genre coming from a place of expertise, being highly trained operatives or experienced investigators, the appeal of their stories comes from the creative ways they resolve massive conflict.

With many action thrillers having adapted their worlds from novels or written work, some of the most memorable franchises have come from source material that established the world and tone of the story, like the Reacher franchise. Others, like John Wick, have come from original spaces, but were inspired by real stories that were then inflated into fictional settings with higher, more intense stakes. Reeves, the star of the John Wick films, is moving into a space with his next project that feels more aligned with the Reacher franchise, despite still being on the big screen in his new film.

Inspired by an upcoming novel by Oliver Lowe, Reeves will star in Kill Current. The novel, which is set to release in May 2027, is the first of a series focusing on Jon Hendricks, a cynical former CIA operative who returns to the field after a mysterious murder brings him to the center of the crime. With Reeves set to star and produce, the upcoming adaptation of Kill Current is giving audiences the chance to jump in on the ground floor.

The first of a new series focused on CIA agent Jon Hendricks, Kill Current sees the former operative having retired from active duty, but returning to the field when his former trainee, Rivers Elliot, disappears. Hendricks looks to find Rivers, but the investigation quickly spirals out of control when a piece of technology that isn't meant to be sustainably used for at least another decade becomes a part of the case. With international travel and a larger geopolitical conflict at hand, things twist and turn for Hendricks throughout the novel, leading him to conclusions he never could've imagined on his own.

With the novel being compared most consistently to the Reacher franchise, Kill Current has echoes of the Lee Child series in its larger story, and has also been compared to John le Carré's work, as well. While Hendricks isn't a carbon copy of Jack Reacher, he definitely has many of the same qualities as the wandering hero, but the technological focus of the series provides a different element to the story. With a planned series in the works, Kill Current is just the opening of what will likely be a far longer story, which could be great for the adaptation side of the franchise.

As someone who's known to take his work seriously, knowing that Reeves is behind the adaptation of Kill Current is an exciting step in the right direction. While it was only announced in September 2026, Kill Current's adaptation has already been pushed into development, which means there's a great chance it comes to fruition. As the first major project from Reeves production company, Two Dragonflies, it's clear that Reeves' involvement in the adaptation is more than just a face for the film. Instead, being on the development side, Reeves is proving that he's bringing his past experiences to the universe in order to create a franchise.

For readers looking for a new thriller series to dive into on the ground floor, Kill Current should be a viable option, especially considering that there's already movement on a film adaptation. With Reeves working on the adaptation in a more extensive way and the novel itself receiving praise as the first a hopefully successful series, Kill Current is prepared to be the next action thriller to reach Reacher and John Wick levels of hype.

Kill Current is available for pre-order through this link.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is a sleek, budget-friendly entry-level smartwatch with effective workout tracking and almost two weeks of battery life. However, initial step counts can be inaccurate, sleep tracking is unreliable, the bulky design won't suit everyone, and there's no third-party app support.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When it comes to finding the best cheap smartwatch, you want something that will suit everything about your lifestyle. Whether it’s sport or running errands, I know I don’t want my watch to get in my way — I need it to support me in my tasks.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is a good choice since it’s affordable and has a sleek design. Fitness tracking is effective, and the battery life is good too. But will it be for everyone? Not by a long shot.

I found the watch face very bulky on my small wrists, and the sleep tracking is inaccurate. The lack of third-party app support may also put off some users. To find out more, keep reading my full CMF Watch 3 Pro review.

Light Green, Orange, Light Grey, Dark Grey

Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Ambient light, Heart rate and SPO2 Blood Oxygen Saturation sensor

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is available to purchase on Amazon for $79 in the U.S. and £99 in the U.K. The watch comes in a range of colors, including Light Green, Orange, Light Grey and Dark Grey, which I tested.

This is a pretty cheap watch and is the same price as the Amazfit Bip 6. Sleep tracking in particular is far more accurate on the Bip 6 in comparison to the CMF, and the Bip 6 can also track more types of workouts.

A cheaper option is the Xiaomi Smart Band 10 for $51, which is much slimmer and will suit people with narrower wrists, as the CMF watch is very chunky.

If you don’t mind being without a screen and want some of the best fitness tracking out there, I’d recommend the Fitbit Air for $99. At just $20 more, it offers incredibly valuable fitness insights. For under $50, you can pick up the Amazfit Band 7, which has a very informative companion app to help improve training where needed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

CMF is a sub-brand of Nothing, and as such, I expected some seriously stunning design work. Whether it’s headphones or milk carton-shaped speakers (CMF Speaker M), Nothing and CMF tech always stands out from the crowd. The CMF Watch 3 Pro is no different.

I tested the Dark Grey version, and I like how this looks for day-to-day wear. However, I felt that the watch face was far too large for my wrist. The circular AMOLED display has a 1.4-inch diameter, so it felt quite bulky. Unfortunately, the Watch 3 Pro doesn’t come in different sizes like the Apple Watch Series 12 or the SE 3 — these are available in multiple case sizes, making them more accessible.

With that said, the strap was secure thanks to the buckle closure. This strap can be removed with a small latch and swapped out for different colors, making customization easy. This was very easy to do when attaching the strap to the watch, but also very secure so it won’t come undone on its own.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro isn’t the brightest out there. The Amazfit Bip 6 can achieve 2,000 nits of brightness, but the CMF only reaches a maximum of 670 nits. It’s bright enough, but if you know you’ll be using the torch feature on the watch face frequently, definitely look at a brighter option like the Bip 6. It will also be hard to see the screen in bright lighting conditions, like running in direct sunshine.

The watch has a durability rating of IP68, meaning it is completely dust-tight and protected against water submersion beyond one meter. That means you can wear it anytime, whether you're working out or at the beach. However, most smartwatches have a durability rating of 5ATM, meaning they can withstand pressure underwater, so you can swim in them, but the CMF watch doesn’t have this level of protection.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro has 131 sport modes and uses built-in dual-band GPS to help you track your routes. It’s easiest to control this through the watch itself, as the app interface is very clunky, and I didn’t feel like I was getting a whole lot of detail, information, or control

I’ve been using the CMF Watch 3 Pro to track hikes, runs, and pilates sessions, and while I feel it’s been tracking my heart rate accurately throughout, I’m not entirely sold. Compared to my phone or Oura Ring 5, step counts, heart rate during workouts and sleep tracking weren’t accurate. This could also be because the watch face was so bulky on my wrist, and this meant that the sensors weren’t always in contact with my skin.

The watch tracks many metrics such as calories burned, step count, distance and of course heart rate, but the information is limited. I didn’t feel like I was getting feedback on my data as I do with other devices like the Amazfit Bip 6. Of course, this is a budget watch, but you get better workout analysis with Garmin, Apple, Amazfit, and even Xiaomi. This was missing from the CMF.

After using the watch for about a week, I started to notice that my movement tracking was improving, and my step counts were becoming more accurate. This likely happened as the watch used information like my height and GPS tracking for distance to affirm the count. It seems like the more it learns about my body, the more accurate it becomes. However, this has never been an issue for my Oura Ring, Apple Watch, or Xiaomi Smart Band, so there’s certainly some improvements to be made here.

The thing I get most excited about when I’m testing out a new fitness tracker is the health and sleep tracking. I track readiness and sleep almost to a fault, so it’s great to see how different devices can inform my health… I just don't think the CMF Watch 3 Pro is the one for the job.

The watch is a decent option for tracking heart health concerns, but shouldn’t be used as a diagnostic tool. It has automatic heart rate measurement that can run for 24 hours a day. It also tracks your resting heart rate throughout the day, and these readings were always about the same as I see with my Oura Ring 5.

You can set up heart rate reminders in the app settings. This means that if your heart rate goes above or below a specified number of beats, it will trigger an alarm. This is a great feature for anyone who may have a health condition. You can also set reminders for drinking water and standing up throughout the day.

I was disappointed by the sleep tracking on this watch. At first, I genuinely thought I was doing something wrong, but a quick look on Reddit and the Nothing community page showed me that this is a pretty common issue. I checked the firmware, battery, my wear position, and restarted the watch, but I was still having trouble logging sleep.

On my first night, the watch only detected three hours of sleep. My Oura Ring and Hatch Sleep clock both told me I was asleep for over eight hours. As I looked further into the data, I saw that the watch had also detected a nap at around eight o’clock in the evening. This was strange since I was cooking dinner, meaning I was moving around and my heart rate would have been slightly elevated.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro does not support any third-party apps; however, you can sync your data with your phone’s health app and directly sync with sports apps such as Strava. The watch also receives your phone's notifications, but you can’t reply to messages directly from the watch.

The dual-band GPS tracking is accurate, and I could see my route after my run. The watch also offers a custom running coach, and this is a great feature for those training towards shorter distances like a 5K or a 10K, but for longer distances I would recommend investing in a running programme that can be entirely tailored to you.

While the watch has some workout analysis, it’s not as in-depth as what you get from brands like Garmin, so if you’re seriously training towards a goal, I’d look into the Garmin Forerunner 70.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro has 13 days of battery life. This is pretty impressive, and about what I’ve come to expect with budget fitness trackers and smartwatches.

The Amazfit Bip 6 lasts for 14 days, and I got 15 days from the Xiaomi Smart Band 10. The CMF watch takes 99 minutes to charge.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is an affordable option for those new to smartwatches and who need something basic to track workouts. The design is sleek, and it’s effective in tracking most workouts, although step counting isn’t accurate at first. The battery life is good, giving almost two weeks of use with a single charge.

Although decent for tracking general health, it can’t track sleep as well as similarly priced rivals like the Xiaomi Smart Band 10. So if you’re someone who likes to make sure they’re getting enough rest, note that sleep tracking is wildly inaccurate. The bulky watch face was far too big for me and got in the way a lot, and unfortunately there isn’t support for third-party apps.

Ashley is a staff writer on the the Reviews team at Tom’s Guide. She has a master’s degree in Magazine Journalism from Cardiff University and a BA in Journalism, Media and Sociology. She has written for titles including Women’s Health UK, writing health and wellness stories, and Virgin Radio UK, specializing in entertainment news and celebrity interviews. She has reported on a variety of topics including music, literature, motorsport, entertainment and health. She has previously reviewed live music events, books, and wellness products but discovering the top audio equipment on the market is what she does best. When she is not testing out the latest tech, you can find her either curled up with a cup of tea and a good novel or out hiking.

#3380. The 6 Most Hopeless Netflix Shows, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

I know a television show has thoroughly destroyed my optimism when somebody receives good news and my first reaction is suspicion. A witness has come forward? Wonderful. Who's going to murder them? The family finally has enough money to escape? Excellent. Which terrible decision will ruin it? I've watched enough fictional people get punished for believing in a better tomorrow that even an innocent smile can make me nervous. Netflix has done it brilliantly, and more than once at that.

And yet, I keep hoping. That's the embarrassing part. I'll spend six episodes watching somebody get crushed by circumstances beyond their control, then convince myself that one brave decision might finally change everything. These shows understand that stubborn little piece of human nature. They make you care enough to believe the impossible, then force you to confront just how difficult it is to escape the world that created the suffering.

Narcos follows the drug lord Pablo Escobar's rise and downfall before turning its attention to the equally powerful Cali Cartel. Pablo Escobar (Wagner Moura) builds a cocaine empire in Colombia, becoming unimaginably wealthy while unleashing violence against anybody threatening his business. American DEA agents Steve Murphy (Boyd Holbrook) and Javier Peña (Pedro Pascal) pursue him through a country where political corruption, cartel influence, and ordinary fear make justice extraordinarily complicated.

There's a terrible irony in watching Escobar's enemies celebrate his death. They've eliminated one extraordinarily dangerous man, but the cocaine business barely hesitates before producing another group of powerful criminals. Peña understands this increasingly well. His attempts to dismantle the Cali Cartel expose uncomfortable connections between traffickers, political interests, and the institutions supposedly fighting them. I particularly admire how the third season makes Jorge Salcedo's desperate attempts to protect his family so nerve-racking. He risks everything to help destroy the organization. Yet even when the major players are brought down, the larger machinery remains. The victory is real. The problem is nowhere near solved.

Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) believes the FBI can understand serial murderers by interviewing them, studying their behavior, and identifying patterns that might help prevent future crimes. Alongside veteran agent Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) and psychologist Wendy Carr (Anna Torv), he begins developing criminal profiling techniques during the late 1970s. Mindhunter makes those interviews

fascinating, particularly when the investigators discover how intelligent, manipulative, and disturbingly ordinary some offenders can appear.

But I find Bill's domestic life even harder to watch than the interviews. His young son becomes involved in a horrifying incident, and Bill's professional expertise offers almost no comfort to his terrified wife Nancy. Here's a man who spends his days examining the psychology of killers but cannot understand what is happening inside his own household. Meanwhile, the Atlanta child-murder investigation exposes the painful limitations of profiling and the pressure surrounding an investigation with grieving families demanding answers. David Fincher's meticulous direction gives this uncertainty an oppressive weight. And those recurring glimpses of the BTK killer? They promise another nightmare the canceled series never got to confront. Two extraordinary seasons, with far too much darkness left unexplored.

Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman) relocates his family from Chicago to Missouri's Lake of the Ozarks after a money-laundering arrangement with a Mexican drug cartel goes catastrophically wrong. His wife Wendy (Laura Linney) gradually becomes an increasingly ruthless partner in their criminal enterprise, while local teenager Ruth Langmore (Julia Garner) gets pulled into their dangerous world. Ozark initially makes the Byrdes' predicament understandable. They're frightened people trying to survive a mistake. Then you notice how comfortable they're becoming with destroying other lives.

Ruth deserved so much better. She grows up surrounded by poverty and criminality, possesses extraordinary intelligence, and spends years struggling to escape the circumstances that shaped her. Watching Garner portray her fury after Wyatt's murder is almost physically painful. And when Ruth finally seems capable of building something independent of the Byrdes, Camila orders her death. The wealthy family survives, having traded its remaining moral integrity for influence and protection. Ruth, who had so much less to begin with, pays the price. I remain furious about it, especially because the ending understands exactly how unfair that outcome is. The Byrdes don't escape corruption. They become powerful enough to live with it.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Korey Wise goes to the police station because he wants to accompany his friend. That apparently harmless decision changes his entire life. In 1989, five Black and Latino teenagers are wrongfully accused of assaulting a woman in New York's Central Park, and investigators pressure them into false confessions. When They See Us follows the boys through their convictions, imprisonment, and the devastating consequences for their families.

Ava DuVernay directed this four-part dramatization with an understanding that wrongful imprisonment destroys far more than a person's freedom. Jharrel Jerome, who portrays Korey as both a teenager and an adult, is extraordinary. Watching him spend years in adult prisons, endure violence, and struggle through solitary confinement is devastating. His mother Dolores (Niecy Nash) keeps loving him across a distance neither of them can overcome. The eventual exonerations bring enormous relief, but I cannot stop thinking about the ordinary experiences these men lost. Birthdays, friendships, relationships, the simple freedom to grow up without fear. Nobody can hand back an adolescence. The legal system finally recognizes their innocence, long after their lives have been permanently changed.

Seong Gi-hun (Lee Jung-jae) is drowning in debt when a mysterious recruiter offers him the opportunity to compete for an enormous cash prize. He enters a competition where childhood games carry fatal consequences, and desperate contestants must decide whether their own survival is worth sacrificing other people. Squid Game initially presents the nightmare as a grotesque contest. Eventually, it becomes clear that the competition merely reproduces the cruelty many participants were already experiencing outside its walls.

I still haven't recovered from Ali's (Anupam Tripathi) betrayal during the marble game. He trusts Sang-woo (Park Hae-soo), believing his friend has discovered a way for them both to survive. Instead, that trust becomes the very thing used against him. And Gi-hun's eventual victory is practically unbearable because everyone he cared about inside the competition is gone. Creator Hwang Dong-hyuk pushes that cruelty further when Gi-hun returns, determined to destroy the games themselves. His rebellion fails, his closest friend Jung-bae (Lee Seo-hwan) is killed, and his attempt to dismantle the organization ends with another devastating sacrifice. If I reveal anything more, it will ruin the show. So just go and watch this masterpiece.

A child disappears from the German town of Winden, and the investigation begins exposing a network of family secrets stretching across generations. Young Jonas Kahnwald (Louis Hofmann) discovers that the caves beneath the town connect different periods of history, allowing people to travel through time. Dark transforms this mystery into an extraordinary tragedy about families whose attempts to protect one another repeatedly become the causes of their own suffering.

There's a conversation between Jonas and his father Michael (Sebastian Rudolph) that I genuinely find unbearable. Jonas has traveled into the past hoping to prevent Michael's suicide. But Michael doesn't yet know he's supposed to kill himself. Imagine going back in time to save somebody you love and discovering that your attempt to protect them may help create the tragedy you're desperate to prevent. That cruel contradiction runs through the entire series. People sacrifice relationships, betray their families, and commit terrible acts because they believe they can change what happens next. Dark leaves you feeling devastated. Even its salvation feels like a farewell to people I desperately wanted to see happy.

#3379. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3378. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3377. Netflix's New 8-Part Psychological Thriller Earns Near-Perfect Rotten Tomatoes Audience Score

Growing up around performers, storytelling was always central to Emma's life. Add in a nerdy older brother who introduced her to Marvel at far too young an age, and her love for entertainment led her to pursue a Journalism degree at Indiana University, where she discovered her passion for entertainment reporting. She spent nearly one year in Los Angeles covering industry stories and fully immersing herself in the world of entertainment media.

Netflix's newest psychological thriller is off to a promising start.

Created by Quinn Shephard, The Body follows a group of Catholic school girls whose dance-team initiation goes wrong, leading to prophetic visions and mass hysteria throughout their town. The psychological thriller stars Kristina Bogic, Geena Meszaros, and Sarah Boustany, alongside High School Musical: The Musical: The Series actor Sofia Wylie, former NFL player Nnamdi Asomugha, and Louisa Krause.

According to Rotten Tomatoes, The Body has earned a 98% audience score from more than 500 ratings. The eight-episode series, which premiered on Netflix on November 11, also holds an 86% critics' score based on 22 reviews, putting its audience rating 12 percentage points above its critical score.

The strong audience reception follows an equally promising start. When The Body premiered on November 11, it debuted with a perfect 100% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes based on six reviews. Although that rating has since dropped as more critics weighed in, the series has continued to receive positive responses, with audiences currently rating it even higher than critics.

In ScreenRant's review of The Body season 1, Dani Kessel Odom gave the psychological thriller a 6/10, calling it a "campy, entertaining hot mess." While praising its religious satire, the review criticized the show's inconsistent pacing and rushed ending.

With only a few days since its release, the Rotten Tomatoes score could still fluctuate as more reviews are submitted. Nevertheless, its near-perfect audience rating gives the Netflix thriller TV show an impressive early reception, particularly as the series combines several genres, including supernatural horror, coming-of-age drama, and psychological suspense.

The series follows a group of teenage girls who pray to the Devil, whom they call the Prince of Darkness, hoping to win their dance-team regionals. However, their ritual involves a human sacrifice, setting off a series of increasingly disturbing events. What begins as a desperate attempt to secure a victory soon develops into a larger mystery involving guilt, friendship, and the supernatural.

In an interview with Netflix's Tudum, Shephard described the series as "gritty camp," reflecting its unusual combination of teenage drama and religious horror. The show's tone also draws inspiration from movies like Carrie, Jennifer's Body, and even Mean Girls, blending supernatural horror with dark humor and teenage drama.

The positive reception also comes as The Body finds instant streaming success on Netflix. At one point, the psychological thriller climbed to No. 2 on Netflix's Top 10 TV shows chart after reaching No. 7 within its first day on the streamer. The series was also trending in 86 countries and ranked as the second most-watched TV show in the United States.

The series marks another television project for Shephard, who previously developed Hulu's true-crime drama Under the Bridge, starring Lily Gladstone and Riley Keough, and wrote and directed the 2022 satirical film Not Okay, starring Zoey Deutch. Both projects explored darker themes, while The Body takes a different approach by incorporating supernatural horror into its coming-of-age story.

Despite its strong audience reception and early streaming success, Netflix has yet to renew The Body for season 2, although its creators have already discussed the show's future. Speaking to TV Insider, co-showrunner Gina Gammell explained that season 1's ending hints at where they "wish to go next season if we're so lucky to get one."

The Body is currently streaming on Netflix.

#3376. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3374. Florence Pugh’s Steinbeck Adaptation Officially Passes Massive Netflix Milestone

East of Eden has reaped a bountiful harvest for Netflix. Not only has the new adaptation of the classic John Steinbeck novel been a critical success, but it's still garnering new viewers. The seven-episode miniseries, which stars Florence Pugh, has just passed a major milestone.

Based on Steinbeck's bestselling 1952 novel, East of Eden is a generational saga that centers around Cathy Ames (Pugh) and Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott). The two meet in the late 19th century when Cathy is found half-dead by half-brothers Adam and Charles (Mike Faist). Trying to overcome their respective dark pasts, Cathy and Adam marry and travel west to California. However, Cathy can't defy her true nature, and abandons Adam with their twin sons, Caleb and Aron, shortly after their births. When the two grow to manhood, they must reckon with the ghosts of their past.

After being released on October 1, East of Eden has now spent six consecutive weeks on Netflix's top ten list. It's an impressive feat for a miniseries based on a novel that's already been adapted into an Oscar-winning film, back in 1955. In fact, there's a familial connection between the two adaptations: Zoe Kazan, who created, co-wrote, co-showran, and produced the miniseries, is the granddaughter of Elia Kazan, who directed the film. It currently holds an 88% Fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes; Collider's Terese Lacson gave it a rave review, calling it "a daring new perspective on the familiar story."

Kazan and co-showrunner Jeb Stuart are moving on from East of Eden to take on a task that's almost as daunting: Larry McMurtry's classic revisionist Western Lonesome Dove. The Pulitzer Prize-winning 1985 novel was already adapted into a much-beloved miniseries in 1989 with Tommy Lee Jones and Robert Duvall. Stuart spoke with Collider about taking on McMurtry's magnum opus, and what the new Netflix adaptation will do that the original didn't: "I have great respect for the original miniseries, and obviously the novel is like East of Eden. It's a big, bold American novel that's...also something you could use as a doorstop, it's 900 pages. Because it is 900 pages, there's a lot they didn't get into that four-episode miniseries that was, you know, Robert Duvall's masterpiece."

East of Eden is now streaming on Netflix. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3373. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3372. Battle Royale Told A More Brutal Version Of The Hunger Games 12 Years Earlier

Japanese cinema offered a rendition of The Hunger Games 12 years earlier, and it’s so much more intense. Young adult dystopian fiction has produced some of the most successful entertainment franchises of the 21st century. Few have made a bigger impression than The Hunger Games, Suzanne Collins' bestselling book series and its hugely successful film adaptations.

The Hunger Games franchise established a distinctive formula for dystopian blockbuster filmmaking, combining political commentary with high-stakes survival drama. However, the idea of forcing young people to fight one another to the death in a government-controlled competition wasn't new when Collins introduced Panem. In fact, a Japanese filmmaker had already explored a remarkably similar premise, taking it in a considerably more violent and disturbing direction.

Released more than a decade before the first Hunger Games movie, Battle Royale is one of the most provocative dystopian movies ever made. Its influence and similarities to Collins' franchise continue to invite comparisons, particularly among those who want something considerably more brutal after finishing Katniss Everdeen's story.

Directed by Kinji Fukasaku in 2000, Battle Royale adapted Koushun Takami's 1999 novel of the same name. The premise will sound immediately familiar to anyone who has watched The Hunger Games: a totalitarian government selects a group of teenagers, transports them to an isolated location, and forces them to fight until only one remains alive. However, while Katniss Everdeen enters the arena as part of a televised competition, the students in Battle Royale are victims of a government program intended to terrorize an increasingly rebellious younger generation.

Battle Royale centers on a class of 42 junior high school students who are abducted during a school trip and transported to an island. Their former teacher, Kitano, explains that they have been selected under the Battle Royale Act, a government policy that forces one school class to participate in a three-day fight to the death. Each student receives supplies and a randomly assigned weapon, while explosive collars ensure nobody can simply refuse to participate or escape.

The basic mechanics are remarkably similar to The Hunger Games, but Fukasaku's film makes the experience considerably less like a sporting event. There are no elaborate opening ceremonies, celebrity stylists, or opportunities to cultivate public affection. The teenagers are simply abandoned with instructions to kill their classmates, and the government expects them to comply.

Rather than turning violence into an elaborate national spectacle, it presents the competition as a bleak institutional punishment designed to demonstrate the consequences of challenging authority.

One of the most obvious differences between Battle Royale and The Hunger Games is their respective approaches to violence. The Hunger Games certainly contains disturbing material, particularly considering its teenage characters, but its PG-13 classification required fairly restrained bloodshed. Fukasaku, meanwhile, makes little effort to soften the brutality.

Students are shot, stabbed, beaten, and blown apart, with Battle Royale frequently emphasizing the physical consequences of each confrontation. Its violence isn't restricted to the anonymous background deaths of characters audiences barely know, either. Fukasaku gives several students individual personalities and relationships before subjecting them to sudden, shocking deaths. The contrast between their ordinary teenage lives and the savagery of the competition is precisely what makes it so uncomfortable.

The sudden deaths reinforce how little control the students have over their circumstances. Even characters who initially appear confident or capable of surviving can be killed within moments, often by people they previously considered friends. The arbitrary distribution of weapons makes matters worse, ensuring that some students begin with a significant advantage over others.

There is also a particularly nasty sense of unpredictability to the film's violence. The Hunger Games establishes a more conventional progression of alliances, confrontations, and strategic eliminations, whereas Battle Royale frequently allows paranoia and panic to dictate what happens next.

Despite their obvious similarities, Battle Royale and The Hunger Games approach their dystopian settings from different political perspectives. Both examine authoritarian governments that maintain control through fear, using young people as instruments of state power. However, The Hunger Games focuses particularly on class inequality, propaganda, and the exploitation of poverty.

Panem's Hunger Games are an annual reminder of the Capitol's victory over the rebellious districts. The wealthy citizens are encouraged to treat the deaths of teenagers as entertainment, while the impoverished districts are forced to sacrifice their children.

Battle Royale, by contrast, focuses more on generational conflict and the breakdown of trust between adults and children. Its fictional government responds to fears about juvenile delinquency by introducing a policy that effectively declares an entire generation expendable. The students are punished collectively, regardless of whether they have actually committed any wrongdoing.

Battle Royale doesn’t present a conventional heroic rebellion but rather examines what happens when a society teaches its children to distrust one another. Its characters are frequently frightened, selfish, impulsive, and emotionally overwhelmed, which makes them seem considerably closer to ordinary teenagers than the increasingly strategic competitors of Panem.

For anyone who loves The Hunger Games, Battle Royale is a perfect next watch because it offers the deadly survival premise in a much less sanitized form. Both put teenagers in situations where survival means confronting people they know, but Battle Royale’s approach makes the psychological and physical consequences much more immediate. There is no glamorous preparation for the competition, no carefully managed public image, and no expectation that the contestants will become celebrities.

The Hunger Games examines how an authoritarian government uses spectacle and propaganda to maintain power, whereas Battle Royale spotlights the destruction of trust between ordinary people. The films also make an interesting double feature because their protagonists respond to institutional cruelty in different ways.

Katniss gradually becomes a symbol of rebellion, while Shuya and Noriko are primarily concerned with surviving. As a result, Battle Royale is particularly valuable for anyone interested in dystopian narratives that don’t adhere to classic Hollywood blockbuster storytelling.

Battle Royale is particularly effective at exploring the emotional consequences of its premise without turning every character into a perfectly calculated survivalist. The friendships, romances, jealousies, and petty disagreements that define school life don't suddenly disappear when the students are given weapons. Instead, those familiar relationships become the foundation for some of the film's most upsetting moments.

Ultimately, Battle Royale deserves to be watched on its own merits rather than simply as the Japanese predecessor to The Hunger Games. Its examination of institutional cruelty, teenage alienation, and the destructive consequences of authoritarianism gives it considerably more substance than its notorious reputation for violence might suggest. Fans of The Hunger Games adventures will recognize plenty of familiar ideas, but Fukasaku's film takes them somewhere much darker.

The Hunger Games is the first of four in the action-drama movie series based on the novels by Suzanne Collins. Set in a dystopian world where people are separated into twelve districts to maintain order, this first film in the franchise focuses on Katniss Everdeen as she is forced to participate in The Hunger Games: a draconian gladiatorial survival event where there can be only one winner.

The dystopian action movie Battle Royale takes place in a future Japan, where a group of high school students fight to the death in a deserted island until only one survivor remains. Directed by Kinji Fukasaku, the 2000 film gave rise to a whole genre of similar stories such as the Hunger Games books and movies, as well as the video game Fortnite.

#3371. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3369. The 7 Best Christmas Movies To Watch in November

'Tis the season to be jolly! Well, almost. As Mariah Carey defrosts and Thanksgiving dinner gets prepped, some Christmas lovers are still eager to haul out the holly and start celebrating. If you’re one of those in that camp and are ready to watch some Christmas movies, we have seven Christmas movies to watch this November to get you in the holiday spirit.

We have a fun batch of films that span the classics through new holiday films that debuted this year. Not every film goes full-throttle Christmas, just in case you’re not ready to trade out the changing of the leaves for some white landscapes. From hilarious holiday gatherings to an action-thriller that sparks annual debates about whether or not it’s a Christmas film, these movies are perfect to jump-start the season!

Let’s begin with the ultimate debate: is Die Hard a Christmas movie? Well, if you’re reading this entry, then you’ve got your answer! Directed by John McTiernan, the 1988 action thriller follows off-duty New York City police detective John McClane (Bruce Willis) as he visits Los Angeles on Christmas Eve to reconcile with his estranged wife. When a team of heavily armed criminals led by Hans Gruber (Alan Rickman) seizes her office building to steal millions in bearer bonds, McClane must wage a solo, barefoot guerrilla war to rescue the holiday party hostages, including his wife, Holly Gennaro-McClane (Bonnie Bedelia).

Watching Die Hard in November is the unofficial kick-off to the holiday movie season because it lets you embrace the Christmas spirit early without committing to traditional sap. The film is perfect for a November viewing because, at its core, it is still a family reconciliation movie about a dad trying to make things right with his estranged wife and kids by Christmas, complete with a Grinch-like corporate villain getting foiled. By checking it off your list in November, you beat the December content overload and stake your claim early in the eternal debate. Who doesn't need an ‘80s-soaked, action-packed shoot-em-up?

It’s very likely Elf gets added to the early Christmas rotation because it is simply pure joy. Plus, now two decades old, it’s been happily passed down to the next generation of kids and kids at heart. Directed by Jon Favreau and written by David Berenbaum, the iconic Christmas comedy tells the story of Buddy Hobbes (Will Ferrell), a human who was accidentally transported to the North Pole as a toddler and raised to adulthood among Santa's (Ed Asner) elves. After realizing he is actually human, the delightfully naive Buddy travels to New York City in full elf attire to find his biological father, Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a cynical children's book publisher on Santa's naughty list.

Elf bridges the gap between autumn cynicism and full-blown holiday magic without demanding heavy solemnity. It captures that exact late-fall-into-winter shift in Manhattan—crisp air, department store window displays going up, and the gradual creep of festive lights—mirroring the exact mood of walking outside in November. It works for both kids who love the candy-cane silliness and adults who appreciate Ferrell's physical comedy, making it an easy crowd-pleaser before holiday schedules get chaotic in December. Favreau designed the movie to combat modern cynicism, infusing it with hand-crafted, Rankin/Bass-inspired North Pole charm rather than high-pressure holiday stress.

Two years ago, Hallmark Channel jump-started a new tradition by capitalizing on a certain pop culture romance involving a mega pop star and her Kansas City Chiefs boyfriend. Well, after that success, they followed it up with a Buffalo Bills-centric Christmas love story. Now, the action is moving to Chicago in Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story. In this story, Avery Clark (Lyndsy Fonseca), an ambitious freelance reporter, returns to Chicago for Christmas and is assigned to write a human-interest piece on a lifelong Chicago Bears superfan, Darlene Donnelly (Marsha Mason), who's about to attend her 500th game. Because she knows next to nothing about football, the superfan’s handsome grandson, Matt Donnelly (Robert Buckley), a local firefighter, steps in to show her what Bears Nation really means.

As with the previous two films, Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story leans heavily into the beauty of fandom through the fanfare of Chicago Bears stadium traditions and crisp autumn-into-winter football weather before Christmas decorations completely take over. A love letter to the Windy City, the film showcases iconic Chicago spots and captures the city's energy. Centered on warm, generational family bonds, Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story lets you kick off your holiday watchlist early in the winter transition, offering comfort, community, and rom-com cheer that unites holiday fans with football lovers.

It’s hard to believe, but this Christmas will be our first without everyone’s favorite mom, Catherine O’Hara, so it’s a perfect time to kick off the holiday season with the beloved classic Home Alone. Directed by Chris Columbus and written by John Hughes, Home Alone follows eight-year-old Kevin McCallister (Macaulay Culkin), who is accidentally left behind in suburban Chicago when his family flies to Paris for a Christmas vacation. While he initially enjoys his newfound freedom, he must protect his home from a pair of bumbling burglars, Harry and Marv (Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern), known as the Wet Bandits.

Home Alone is a perfect November watch that has become a seasonal gateway tradition. The comfort film combines chaotic family dynamics with pure childhood wish-fulfillment. You get glowing Chicago neighborhood lights, snow-dusted streets, and a John Williams score that eases you into the holidays. Home Alone strips away the heavy focus on Santa or presents, focusing instead on themes of independence, overcoming fear, and finding your way back to family. Beneath the slapstick booby traps, Kevin's journey delivers pure warmth. If you love Home Alone and you’re eager for more, thankfully, there's an equally delightful sequel, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York!

If there’s ever been a film for all seasons, it’s Meet Me in St. Louis. But let’s face it, it qualifies as a Christmas movie because of the iconic rendition of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.” Directed by Vincente Minnelli, the classic follows a year in the life of the upper-middle-class Smith family as they navigate romance, family bonds, and everyday dilemmas in turn-of-the-century Missouri. Divided into seasonal vignettes, the narrative builds anticipation for the upcoming 1904 World's Fair until the father, Alonzo (Leon Ames), announces a sudden corporate relocation to New York City.

Meet Me in St. Louis is the ideal transition-season film to watch in November because it literally covers an entire calendar year, moving gracefully through summer, autumn, Halloween, and Christmas, rather than diving straight into snow and Santa Claus. The iconic film starring Judy Garland treats November as an awkward purgatory before eventually building toward its famous holiday climax. It lets you slowly open the door to the Christmas season, highlighting why it draws such anticipation. The centerpiece is Garland’s Esther Smith singing the beloved Christmas classic to her heartbroken little sister, Tootie (Margaret O’Brien), as the family faces a dreaded move to New York City.

While the title The 12 Dates of Christmas may sound familiar, this is a brand-new film for 2026. The romantic holiday comedy follows Christina Walker (Lucy Hale), a successful business owner who has consistently prioritized her career over her personal life. After facing pressure from her family at the holidays, she pledges to find a partner and embarks on a plan to go on 12 blind dates in the 12 weeks leading up to Christmas Eve. Along the way, she navigates a series of hilariously disastrous setups while unexpectedly crossing paths with an old high school crush, Peter Grant (Ian Harding).

The 12 Dates of Christmas is an ideal early-November holiday watch because its core premise literally maps out a slow-burn countdown to December. Sometimes, the best Christmas movies to watch before December are the ones that are considered low-stakes guilty pleasures. This film is a light, breezy transition into festive viewing without plunging you straight into heavy-duty December tinsel overload. A big draw is the Pretty Little Liars reunion. Seeing Hale and Harding reunite on-screen gives it a cozy, familiar comfort-watch energy that matches the urge to curl up indoors as the weather turns.

With the sequel on the way, it’s the perfect time to revisit The Family Stone. Written and directed by Thomas Bezucha, the family dramedy centers on the ultra-liberal, bohemian New England Stone family whose dynamics are upended when their eldest son, Everett (Dermot Mulroney), brings his rigid, corporate girlfriend, Meredith Morton (Sarah Jessica Parker), home for Christmas. Overwhelmed by the family's hostile reception, she calls her easygoing sister, Julie (Claire Danes), for backup, which triggers a chaotic chain of events and unexpected romantic partner-swapping within the household.

The Family Stone captures the pre-holiday dread and messy human friction of going home for the holidays before the sugar-coated magic of December sets in. November marks the start of the holiday travel gauntlet, and the film leans into the immediate, sweaty-palmed anxiety of meeting a partner’s intensely tight-knit, unfiltered family for the first time. Watching it in November lets you process the emotional weight of family gatherings before you are sitting across from your relatives at the dinner table. With a star-studded ensemble including Diane Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Craig T. Nelson, and Luke Wilson, the film is a fun watch of icons having a blast together.
