#3343. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3340. The 10 Most Hopeless Christmas Movies, Ranked

There’s no shortage of feel-good Christmas movies. Some will have dramatic moments, sure, but you can’t really call It’s a Wonderful Life downbeat or hopeless when it ends up feeling life-affirming and hopeful by the end. So, it’s not a movie that you'll see mentioned below, nor will you see other movies that have a lot of drama but wholly inspiring endings (see also most adaptations of A Christmas Carol).

Instead, what you'll see below are the most hopeless Christmas movies of all time. They generally work as good anti-Christmas movies, telling darker stories that just so happen to play out during the holiday season. They're not all 100% heavy, because some are more cynical than tragic, though in one way or another, they do ultimately stand out against the more conventional Christmas movies out there that you’ve probably seen discussed (and recommended) to death.

The Ref is a well-made comedic crime film that just so happens to take place on Christmas Eve, and mostly concerns a bunch of generally unlikable characters clashing, and then it’s kind of funny because no one’s sympathetic. If you take a step back, or try to imagine yourself stuck in this film, then it would be miserable, and that sense of it all being cynical is what makes it clash with most Christmas movies and the sentiments found within them.

There is certainly a time and place for anti-Christmas movies, especially if you're not someone who feels like engaging with the season this year, for whatever reason.

The antagonist here is a burglar who takes a family hostage, but the family is a dysfunctional one, and everyone ends up making everyone feel worse. There is certainly a time and place for anti-Christmas movies, especially if you're not someone who feels like engaging with the season this year, for whatever reason, and so something pessimistic like The Ref has got your back, in that instance.

What do you want, or what were you expecting? It’s a movie called Bad Santa. Okay, Bad Santa is good, but it’s not really feel-good; that’s the unsurprising part. It’s one of the better R-rated Christmas movies out there, and it might also be one of the “most R-rated” Christmas movies, too, because it's about a miserable conman who robs department stores while dressed up as a mall Santa, and then things change for him to some extent when he meets a young kid who’s struggling socially.

Only “to some extent,” since it’s not really warm and fuzzy, by any means. There is a tiny bit of heart here that stops this from being utterly depressing and nihilistic, yet a lot of the humor comes from that, and Billy Bob Thornton is very much the right person to cast if you want that kind of energy, too. It might not be the kind of dark Christmas movie that'll appeal to everyone, for obvious reasons, but it will likely appeal to you if you're after a Christmas-themed dark comedy.

There were a ton of great movies released in 1984, including Gremlins. This is also an all-timer if you're looking at subversive and possibly "edgy" Christmas movies, and sure, while it’s not as dark or twisted as some other films here, it’s a pretty wild one for something that’s kind of family-friendly. It’s grisly for something that older kids could probably still watch, and the way it goes from being very jolly and cozy to violent and chaotic is great.

The plot… you know the plot, right? It’s Gremlins. It’s a creature feature, and one of the best ever made. It's a dark and very funny film that's willing to strip away some of the typical magic of Christmas, in turn crafting something wilder and weirder than most Christmas movies. And it memorably ruins the magic of Christmas for potential younger viewers, thanks to having a character monologue about the awful event in her life that made her realize Santa wasn’t real. Merry Christmas!

This one is only slightly a Christmas movie, lacking the iconography and warmth you'd associate with such a film, but still, The Lion in Winter is worthy of getting a shout-out here. The premise does ultimately concern a dysfunctional family coming together for the holiday season and arguing a great deal, since they're not just any family, but the royal one, and the King, Henry II, has a few heirs who are power-hungry.

It’s like Succession but set a bit over eight centuries ago, though it doesn’t really feel like your average period drama, because there’s a lot of energy here and an incredible script that feels more modern (but not in a distracting way). The Lion in Winter is excellent as a film on its own, and so maybe the Christmas stuff kind of comes second, but the quality of it overall makes it feel hard to overlook. And, once more, it’s a good anti-Christmas movie, especially if you don’t particularly love the yearly requirement to come together as a family.

There’s one other Christmas-themed slasher movie that’ll be mentioned further down, because it is admittedly more intense and harrowing than Black Christmas. To some extent, Black Christmas is slightly cozy, but it is also tense for its time, not to mention important in the overall history of the slasher genre, since Black Christmas pre-dated other slashers like the original Halloween and Friday the 13th movies by a few years.

Pretty wild to consider there was an essential Christmas slasher movie before there was a true “Halloween” slasher movie; not the holiday you'd expect to be prioritized. Anyway, it’s about the members of a sorority house getting tormented and eventually hunted down by a mysterious killer. Simple stuff, but it’s a slasher movie, so of course it’s not going to be complicated. Black Christmas does what it needs to, and it also did so before a good many other slasher films. Much of it holds up, too (don’t bother with the more recent remakes/updates).

Batman Returns confirms that Gotham City celebrates Christmas. The film plays out when things are snowy and festive, and then it’s notably also quite dark for a superhero movie of its era. 1989’s Batman was already more intense than much of what came before, but Batman Returns is next-level in that regard, pushing things about as far as they can go while (just) retaining a PG-13 rating.

It’s almost a bit much. And sure, other movies here have more violence and profanity, but all this unpleasantness feels a little different in a film like this. So, Batman Returns is more of a cult thing, but the people who do feel this is a cult classic are passionate about Batman Returns; make no mistake. And even if you don’t love it, or enjoy it, it’s not hard to admire how gutsy this one was, and how effectively anti-Christmas it feels among Christmas movies.

Eyes Wide Shut was the final film Stanley Kubrick ever directed, and it came out posthumously. It is kind of a Christmas movie, taking place at the end of the year and having some of the iconography you'd expect to see, but thematically, it’s not very Christmassy. Nor does it really scream Christmas narratively, since it’s about a man putting himself in great danger psychologically and physically when he spirals after learning his wife once thought about cheating on him.

What happens around the middle of Eyes Wide Shut is absolutely horrifying, and then the final act is about the aftermath of all that, and unsettling in more subdued ways. It’s one of the more anxiety-provoking movies of its era for sure, but it is great, both for its direction and for how well-acted it is (Tom Cruise especially seems willing to do just about anything Kubrick asked of him, so he gives one of his most committed performances here).

With Terrifier 3, you get more Terrifier, for better or worse. It’s Terrifier set around Christmastime, so Art the Clown does some of his rampage while being dressed like Santa Claus, and after doing something (expectedly) horrifying to another person dressed up as Santa. You know the drill. Art torments people. Art tortures people. Art (eventually) kills people, after they’ve experienced the most pain possible.

Beyond the bloodshed, there are a few things going on narratively, at least more so than the first movie, and as a continuation of the second movie (also better than the first), Terrifier 3 works pretty well. You shouldn’t watch it if you're even a tiny bit squeamish, and there is a whole lot of gore and stress here, but these are all extreme horror movies, so if you’ve been fooled by Terrifier three times now, hoping for something different each time a new one comes out… like, come on.

The main reason to watch Spencer is Kristen Stewart’s performance as Princess Diana, though you could also watch it if you like Christmas movies but don’t want to watch a nice/happy Christmas movie. It takes place during the holiday season, and is focused on Diana struggling with her marriage and being wrapped up in the royal family, with no one in the institution coming away from things looking particularly good (other than Princess Diana and maybe her two songs).

It's an unrelenting historical drama, but it gets heavy and feels intensely solemn for a good reason, demystifying things and being empathetic toward Diana. Spencer is no ordinary biopic, both because it’s quite dark and also because the timeframe here is rather narrow, but it’s pretty great for what it does and how intense it ends up being. And, once more, Stewart hasn’t even been better than she is here in the lead role.

You have to squint more than usual to see this as a Christmas movie, even compared to some of the other films here, but Brazil takes place at the year’s end, and there’s some Christmas-like imagery. It’s easier to describe as an essential cult classic sci-fi film, and also a very dark comedy, being about a bureaucrat whose life absolutely spirals out of control, largely due to his world being terrible and his luck being even worse.

The line between reality and fantasy breaks down, though not to the extent that you ever entirely forget just how horrible the dystopian world Brazil takes place in truly is. The way it wraps up is especially soul-crushing, and though before that point, much of Brazil is comedic, it’s also an exhausting sort of comedy. If you don’t like feeling more stressed than usual around Christmas, maybe it’s better to wait and watch this one at a different point in the year.

#3339. New Apple TV 4K remote’s best feature requires a newer iPhone model

A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

If you’re interested in the new Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

The most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

You can use the new Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the new speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the new Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

#3338. Timothy Olyphant & Brad Pitt's New Netflix Crime Movie Officially Continues Rating Tradition 7 Years Later

Credit: Marion Curtis/StarPix for Apple TV/INSTARimages

Timothy Olyphant and Brad Pitt's reunion continues a seven-year tradition.

Quentin Tarantino directed the 2019 hit drama Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Pitt, and Margot Robbie. The story unveiled a fictionalized account of the Sharon Tate murders, in which Pitt portrays the stunt double Cliff Booth, who comes across the Manson Family. After the role won him an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor, his character now becomes the hero of his own story in the upcoming sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The only other actor returning is Olyphant, who portrayed the real-life actor James Stacy.

Just weeks before its IMAX release, FilmRatings.com confirmed that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will officially be rated R, like the original 2019 movie. The certificate indicates that the upcoming sequel has "some strong/disturbing violence, bloody images, pervasive language, sexual content, nudity and drug use." The warning is not far off from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, which had similar cautions of its violent content. Nevertheless, the R-rating was expected, given that Netflix released a red-band trailer earlier this month.

It's the latest Olyphant movie to get an R rating. Since Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, only two of his films have avoided the restricted MPA rating; The Starling was rated PG-13, and LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian was TV-Y7-FV.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth takes place eight years after Tarantino's original hit, in which Cliff leaves the stunt world behind and becomes a studio fixer. Before that, the stunt double survived the Manson family attack at the end of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, which hinted at Rick Dalton's acting struggles during the late 1960s. Although Tarantino wrote the story, the directorial duties were passed over to acclaimed director David Fincher.

The upcoming movie marks the fourth reunion between Pitt and Fincher after they previously worked on Se7en, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, and Fight Club. Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Carla Gugino round out the supporting cast.

Olyphant provided details about his appearance and his collaboration with Fincher. He confirmed that his screen time is brief, having just filmed a day and a half of scenes. Nevertheless, he described the sequel as a "cool mix" of both filmmakers, with Tarantino's slick dialogue and Fincher's layered, distinct direction.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will become the first Netflix movie to have an exclusive IMAX release. The sequel is Tarantino and Fincher's most expensive movie, with a $200 million budget. Although DiCaprio had a key role as Rick Dalton in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, he will not reprise the fictional character in the sequel after turning down a cameo.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will be exclusively in IMAX for two weeks, starting November 25, before going to Netflix on December 23.

Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.

The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server.

Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details:

Apple is working on a new app called HarborHarbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf

As the post notes, here’s what the app does:

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.

#3335. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

#3333. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3331. Prime Video's 62-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Deserves Credit For Skipping To Book 2

According to conventional wisdom, the more faithful a live-action adaptation remains to its source material, the more acclaim will be headed its way. That's certainly true for The Expanse, which started on Syfy before moving onto Prime Video halfway through. The future-set space opera rendered James S.A. Corey's novel series in glorious live-action, knowing exactly which parts of the books could be trimmed out, condensed, or tweaked in ways that would remodel the story for a visual medium without feeling like huge deviations.

Generally speaking, TV series based on books and comics start off relatively close to the original story, then forge their own separate path as the show unfolds. The Umbrella Academy, Game of Thrones, and The Walking Dead are all examples of series that grew increasingly confident in ignoring the instruction manual.

The Expanse worked in the opposite direction. The show's six-season run covered Corey's first six books, averaging out at one book per season, and by the time Amazon got hold of it, The Expanse literally was adapting one specific book in each season. During the Syfy days, however, those lines were a little more blurred, and not without good reason.

The Expanse's TV incarnation is known for its blend of space adventuring and interplanetary politics that has earned it such accolades as 'Game of Thrones in space.' While the books adopt a similar mashup of styles, that wasn't the case in James S.A. Corey's debut, Leviathan Wakes.

That first book only followed the narratives of James Holden, leading his crew aboard the Rocinante, and Detective Miller, investigating the disappearance of Julie Mao before fatefully joining up with Holden. The Expanse's first book is actually very light on political intrigue, with characters such as Chrisjen Avasarala and Sadovir Errinwright forced to wait until the sequel, Cibola Burn, before making their respective bows.

Instead of leaving them hanging around for season 2, The Expanse's TV series got Avasarala and Errinwright involved right from the start, adding in new plot points (such as the character of Franklin DeGraaf) to show the unseen politics that happened entirely in the background of book one.

The Expanse's first season mixed the thriller-y excitement of Leviathan Wakes with the slow-burn conspiracies and careful maneuvering of Cibola Burn, and this was undoubtedly the right call. It gave The Expanse's early episodes a more balanced palette, and one that would feel consistent with the seasons to come. Had that initial run of episodes followed the book's full-throttle approach directly, viewers would've been in for an abrupt switch of genres when season 2 started taking a deeper interest in the nitty-gritty of diplomacy.

Bringing Earth politics into The Expanse season 1 inevitably meant parts of Leviathan Wakes were delayed until season 2, which was great news for a certain Josepheus Miller.

The Expanse's first book concludes with Miller crashing Eros onto Venus, and his physical form dying in the process. The Expanse season 1, however, merely ended with Miller escaping Eros alongside Holden and joining the Rocinante crew as a temporary member. Not only did this allow Thomas Jane an extra season on the show, it meant The Expanse retained the noir-ish, 'private detective with a grudge' vibe that tagged along behind Miller, at least for a little while longer.

The TV series enjoyed more tonal consistency as a result, and as great as they are, the first entries in the book series are a lot starker in their leaps between genres. It's not a huge issue on the page, but would have made for a jarring experience in a TV adaptation, and The Expanse deserves all the credit for spotting that potential pitfall in advance.

I’ve been testing the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots for the last month on all of my hikes, and they’ve proved to be some of the best hiking boots for any season and any terrain. They look the part too, which helps me feel unstoppable on the trail.

Mocha/Redwood, Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood, Gravel/Cypress

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are available to purchase on the La Sportiva website for $249 in the U.S. and £220 in the U.K. The color selection differs between territories. In the U.S., there are only two choices — Carbon/Redwood or Mocha/Redwood — and in the U.K. you can choose from Cypress/Azalea, Carbon/Redwood or Gravel/Cypress. You can also purchase the shoes on Amazon for $310 in the U.S., but sizes and colors are limited.

When deciding on the boot size, you will need to convert from European sizing, since this is how the boots are sold on the site. The boots are available in women’s EUR sizes 36 to 42.5 with half sizes, and men’s EUR sizes 40 to 48.5 with half sizes. I’m usually a U.K. size 5 and needed to size up since the boots have a very snug fit. I ended up purchasing an EUR size 39, which is a U.K. size 6 and a U.S. women’s size 7.5.

These boots are certainly on the more expensive side, but it’s not hard to see why. They’re very well made and comfortable to walk in. Also very supportive are the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX. These boots cost $240, but this is the price to pay for a boot you’d happily spend your life walking in.

Another boot with excellent ankle support is the Keen Targhee IV, which costs $169. They’ve been my go-to boots for taking on the outdoors for over a year now, but I think the La Sportivas could end their reign.

After speaking to friends and colleagues, it turns out the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots are a bit like cilantro — you either love it, or you hate it with a burning passion. But to me, they’re perfect. I like the look of the boots and the available colorways. They look like they mean business when you’re out on the trail.

The boots are perfect for narrow feet, and lace up for a snug, albeit supportive, fit. However, there’s no wide fit option, so those with wide feet need to look elsewhere, such as the Keen Targhee IV.

The upper is made from nubuck leather and a breathable Gore-Tex lining for a water-resistant finish. They coped well with heavy rain and deep puddles, and are also tear-resistant, so they can withstand even the rockiest terrain. The lacing system is very supportive, and cinched in all the right places to ensure a comfortable walk.

Although the laces get tight, my ankles moved freely. In other boots, I’ve been used to having a limited range of movement around my ankles like the Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid GTX, but these felt a lot more forgiving.

The La Sportiva boots have a footbed boost of 5mm, which is simply the insole height. This contributes to the cushioning of the boot and felt like it contoured to my feet. The drop value of 8mm (from heel to toe) also helped me get the best posture possible.

Usually, in other boots, I experience some strain on my lower back as a result of a smaller drop value, as there’s more pressure on my calves. Instead, I felt supported. The flex system with the CM EVE foam (a lightweight, rubber foam) also helps with rebound.

The outsole provided me with a lot of grip for every terrain I walked on. The lugs of the boot, which dig into the ground to provide traction, measure 4.5mm tall. This is a good height for grip and I find it to be the sweet spot, with most of my Keen boots also sitting in this range. The soles are made of Vibram rubber, so they absorb a lot of the impact of the ground, which helped reduce strain when walking over longer distances.

I have no complaints about the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots and their comfort level. I wore them right out of the box with no issues. My first walk in these boots took me through gravel, muddy fields, and shallow running water. The traction and flex felt great right off the bat.

The toe box of the boots is quite narrow, but this really wasn’t an issue for me. In fact, since my feet are very narrow, the ideal fit gave me more control, providing a more stable hiking experience.

My only very slight qualm is that my feet naturally swell from heat when walking, so the boots can start to feel a little tight. It’s obviously good that the lace-up system doesn’t slip, but sometimes, a little bit of give is a good thing, as you can move more freely. With that said, it didn’t cause me any major pain or blisters.

Cushioning in these boots is ideal. It took away some of the impact, especially when walking over bigger rocks and generally rough terrain, but I could still feel what was going on underfoot. The Scarpa Cyrus 2 Mid boots also let you feel the ground beneath your feet through the soles, and this is a feature I’ve come to really appreciate.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easily some of my favorite boots.. They’re comfortable, cushioned, and support me across any terrain. The cushioning helps support my knees by reducing impact.

The 4.5mm lugs on the outsole of the hiking boots made me feel stable across all terrain I walked on. Even on slippery surfaces like wet rocks, the Vibram soles provided a lot of grip, and I didn’t slip once despite my clumsy disposition.

The arch support is great, and this in turn improved my posture. Since the lace-up system is tight for narrow feet, I felt a lot of support from the side walls — these two things combined stopped my feet from turning inward as I walked and boosted protection for my ankles by increasing my overall stability.

The boots have a moderate amount of flex, but never bent too much. I had complete support where I needed it. The most flex is happening in the toe box, which worked perfectly for me, especially when navigating uneven, tricky terrain.

Waterproofing on the La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX boots is very effective. I went out hiking in the pouring rain, and my socks stayed completely dry. My walk also took me through puddles and shallow running water, and luckily my feet stayed dry and warm. I know I’ll be able to rely on these boots for all seasons.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are easy to maintain, just like any other leather boot. If they get muddy on the trail, remove the laces and gently brush off any dry mud. Then, use a damp cloth to remove any stubborn stains. Let the boots air-dry naturally and avoid artificial heat, as it can compromise the boot's integrity.

The La Sportiva TX5 Evo Mid GTX hiking boots are some of my favorite boots. They were comfortable and ready for a long walk right out of the box, and felt durable, even on trickier terrain. The boots provided excellent traction and stability across mud, gravel, and sand, and the waterproofing withstood stormy weather.

Although the cushioning and support are good, it’s worth noting that the boots fit narrowly. For people with wider feet, this boot simply won’t fit even if you size up, and unfortunately, La Sportiva doesn’t offer a wide fit option.

Nevertheless, this is still a great all-rounder boot to support you on the toughest adventures, and one I certainly recommend.

#3328. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

#3326. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

#3325. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3324. Amy Poehler’s ‘Parks and Recreation’ Replacement Officially Arrives Next Week

It's been over ten years since Amy Poehler left Pawnee, Indiana, and Parks and Recreation behind, and since then, she's been less of a defining presence in live-action television comedy. Her most recognizable role since starring in the beloved mockumentary sitcom for seven seasons has easily been as the emotion Joy in Disney's Inside Out movies, though she's also been quite busy behind the camera. She co-created the Netflix hit Russian Doll, as well as her own animated comedy series, Duncanville, and served as producer on everything from Broad City to Harlem and the recent Cinderella-twisting animated film Steps. In just over a week, however, she'll be back to bringing the laughs on-screen with help from a familiar collaborator.

Poehler is set to resurface at Peacock for the new series Dig, which she both leads and co-created with one half of the Parks and Recreation creative duo, Michael Schur​​​​. Based on Kate Myers' bestselling novel Excavations, it centers on four women at vastly different stages of their careers working on an archaeological dig site in Greece over the summer who set their differences aside after making the discovery of a lifetime. Their history-changing big break also puts them at the center of an international conspiracy that spans far wider than they could possibly imagine. All episodes are slated to drop on November 23, just in time for a holiday binge over Thanksgiving.

After leading Pawnee's Parks and Recreation department, Poehler leads the cast of Dig as the excavation site's lead archaeologist, Elise, with Hugh Laurie playing the long-standing source of her ire, Neville, a British scientist who sincerely loves archaeology but has simply refused to retire from the dig and always gets the credit for any discoveries. The main group is rounded out by Geraldine Viswanathan, Fina Strazza, and Antonia Thomas, though there's also a wealth of stars attached. Jason Mantzoukas, Noma Dumezweni, and Brennan Lee Mulligan are set to recur, while What We Do in the Shadows alum Kayvan Novak headlines a group of guest stars including Max Greenfield, Jon Pointing, Bonita Friedericy, and Dan Bucatinsky.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

#3323. CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features

Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

#3321. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3320. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

You can watch iFixit’s full teardown below:

#3316. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3314. Every Season of 'The Bear,' Ranked Worst to Best

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

I have never wanted to hug a group of fictional people and tell them to shut the hell up quite as badly as I do with the staff of The Bear. These people can turn a perfectly normal conversation into a personal insult in under twenty seconds. Somebody asks for help, somebody else hears criticism, and suddenly three generations of unresolved family trauma are being discussed over a pan of burning food. I adore them. I also find them exhausting.

And that's why I'm so particular about this show. I don't need everyone to become emotionally healthy or start speaking politely. I need their mistakes to lead somewhere. I need the affection underneath all that anger to feel earned. Across five seasons, the series has sometimes tested my patience, occasionally broken my heart, and delivered a few hours of television I would defend against practically anything. Christopher Storer made this series for FX on Hulu and clearly let us know from the beginning that the restaurant was an extension of this family's emotional wreckage. Let’s further dig in.

Carmy Berzatto (Jeremy Allen White) has spent so long trying to build the perfect restaurant that he's nearly destroyed his relationships with the people helping him. Season 4 finally forces him to confront that contradiction. Sydney (Ayo Edebiri) is considering an opportunity outside the restaurant, Uncle Jimmy's financial pressure is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore, and the kitchen desperately needs Carmy to stop treating every imperfect detail like a personal catastrophe.

I wanted to love this season more. There are beautiful moments, particularly Sydney's conversations with her father and the uncomfortable honesty of Carmy's decision to leave the restaurant behind. But too much of the storytelling feels hesitant, as though everyone is approaching an important realization without quite getting there. Even the strongest emotional exchanges sometimes arrive after hours of familiar frustration. I respect where Carmy's story goes. I just wish the journey there had been considerably more exciting.

I'll defend “Napkins” against almost any criticism you throw at this season. Tina (Liza Colón-Zayas) loses her job, spends a miserable day searching for another, and eventually wanders into the Beef. There, Mikey (Jon Bernthal) offers her something she's been denied everywhere else that day: a little kindness. Their conversation is painfully ordinary, which is precisely why it hits so hard. Ayo Edebiri directed the episode, and that quiet meeting accomplishes more than some of the season's elaborate restaurant scenes.

Then “Ice Chips” puts Natalie (Abby Elliott) in labor with her deeply unreliable mother Donna (Jamie Lee Curtis) beside her. Two women who've spent years hurting and misunderstanding each other suddenly have nowhere to hide. I love these episodes desperately. Unfortunately, Carmy's obsessive pursuit of perfection grows repetitive, while the restaurant's larger story often struggles to move forward. Season 3 can be maddeningly self-indulgent. Yet those two intimate stories remind me just how extraordinary this show can be when it allows somebody other than Carmy to occupy the emotional center.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

An enormous storm, a booking disaster, dwindling supplies, and an overloaded dining room. Oh, and the chef who helped build the restaurant has announced he's leaving. Season 5 gives Sydney, Richie (Ebon Moss-Bachrach), and the remaining team one monstrous service to prove they can manage without Carmy. I love that premise. After spending years watching these people discuss the possibility of becoming better, we finally get to see whether they've actually learned anything.

The pressure is magnificent, particularly when improvisation replaces Carmy's obsession with absolute control. Tina gets opportunities to demonstrate her confidence, Sydney starts trusting her own leadership, and Richie increasingly resembles somebody who genuinely belongs in hospitality. There's a wonderful sense that this restaurant has become larger than the man who created it. The season's final gathering is affectionate enough to make me forgive some of its more sentimental impulses. And Carmy's last message to Mikey, simply saying “All good,” is devastating in its simplicity. Five seasons of grief, anger, and impossible expectations, reduced to two words that finally sound like peace.

The Original Beef of Chicagoland is a disaster. The kitchen is filthy, the accounts are a nightmare, the employees refuse to cooperate, and Carmen has inherited the entire operation following his brother's suicide. He knows how to cook at an extraordinary level. Unfortunately, knowing how to run a prestigious kitchen doesn't prepare him for managing people who loved Mikey and resent practically everything Carmy represents.

I'll never forget “Review.” Online orders keep pouring from the printer, Sydney's attempts to improve the operation collapse into chaos, and Carmy finally loses control. It's an agonizing episode because everybody is contributing to the disaster, yet nobody has enough perspective to stop it. And underneath all that shouting is a grieving younger brother desperately trying to understand why Mikey left him behind. When Carmy eventually finds Mikey's note and the money hidden inside those tomato cans, I feel relief every single time. For a brief moment, these exhausted people have something worth celebrating together.

Finally, my favorite. Richie is assigned to polish forks at an elite restaurant, and I genuinely believe the resulting episode, “Forks,” belongs among the greatest hours of television in recent memory. Here's a man who's spent years defending his own importance through arguments, resentment, and sheer stubbornness. Then somebody teaches him that taking care of other people can be an extraordinary profession. Ebon Moss-Bachrach makes Richie's growing pride almost unbearably touching. That moment when he drives through Chicago singing along to Taylor Swift? I could watch it a hundred times.

And that's only one part of an astonishing season. The old sandwich shop is being transformed into a fine-dining restaurant, with Sydney, Marcus (Lionel Boyce), and the others pursuing skills they never imagined possessing. “Fishes” takes us into a Berzatto family Christmas dinner so hostile that Donna eventually drives her car into the house. Watching it makes every argument in the present more understandable. Then the restaurant finally opens, and Carmy ends up trapped inside the walk-in refrigerator, unable to participate in the success he's sacrificed everything to achieve. That contradiction breaks my heart. Everybody else is discovering what they can become, while Carmy still cannot imagine happiness without finding a way to punish himself. Season 2 understands these people completely. I wouldn't trade a single one of its extraordinary emotional highs for a tidier, more comfortable story.
